study.note: Six weeks of antibiotics were not inferior to 12 weeks for curing bacterial infection of the spine.

name: Septic arthritis
sx: A single hot, swollen, very painful joint
about: Bacteria infect a joint, often the knee, and enzymes from bacteria and immune cells can destroy cartilage within days. It is treated as an emergency with joint drainage and antibiotics. Gonococcus is a cause in sexually active young adults.

study.title: Oral versus Intravenous Antibiotics for Bone and Joint Infection
study.note: In bone and joint infections, oral antibiotics in the first 6 weeks were noninferior to IV antibiotics for treatment failure at 1 year.

name: Achilles tendon rupture
sx: A sudden 'pop' at the back of the ankle, like being kicked
Sharp pain at the back of the heel
A gap felt in the tendon
Foot doesn't move when the calf is squeezed
about: The body's strongest tendon tears, usually during a sudden push-off in sports, often in middle-aged weekend athletes. Squeezing the calf normally points the foot downward, and when that fails the tendon is torn (Thompson test). Fluoroquinolone antibiotics raise the risk.

study.title: Nonoperative or Surgical Treatment of Acute Achilles' Tendon Rupture
study.note: Surgery did not give better results than nonoperative treatment at 12 months for an acute Achilles tendon rupture.

name: Compartment syndrome
sx: Pain far worse than the injury seems to justify
Pain when the muscle is passively stretched
about: Swelling inside a closed muscle compartment, often after a fracture or crush injury, raises pressure until blood can't flow in. Muscle and nerve begin to die within hours. Surgeons cut open the tight fascia (fasciotomy) to relieve it. A missing pulse is a late sign.

study.title: Intramuscular pressures with limb compression. Clarification of the pathogenesis of the drug-induced muscle-compartment syndrome
study.note: Measured very high muscle pressures in limbs compressed under the body during drug-induced coma, enough to block circulation and start compartment and crush syndromes.

name: Psoriasis
sx: Thick red patches with silvery scales
Patches on the elbows, knees and scalp
about: An immune-driven disease in which IL-17 and IL-23 signaling makes skin cells multiply in days instead of weeks, piling up as scaly plaques. About a third of patients develop psoriatic arthritis. It is not contagious.

study.title: Oral Icotrokinra for Plaque Psoriasis in Adults and Adolescents
study.note: An oral peptide that blocks the IL-23 receptor, icotrokinra, cleared skin far more often than placebo at 16 weeks in moderate-to-severe psoriasis.

name: Atopic dermatitis (eczema)
sx: Rash in the creases of elbows and knees
Often alongside asthma or hay fever
about: A weakened skin barrier, often from variants in the filaggrin gene, lets in irritants and allergens and lets water out, which drives type 2 immune inflammation. It usually starts in childhood and is part of the 'atopic march' with food allergy, asthma and hay fever.

study.title: Two Phase 3 Trials of Dupilumab versus Placebo in Atopic Dermatitis
study.note: Dupilumab, which blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signaling, improved eczema signs, itch, anxiety and depression symptoms and quality of life compared with placebo.

name: Acne vulgaris
sx: On the face, chest and back
about: Hair follicles clog with oil (sebum) and dead skin cells, and Cutibacterium acnes bacteria multiply inside, triggering inflammation. Androgens boost oil production, which is why acne surges at puberty. It affects most teenagers.

study.title: Effectiveness of spironolactone for women with acne vulgaris (SAFA) in England and Wales: pragmatic, multicentre, phase 3, double blind, randomised controlled trial
study.note: The hormone-blocking drug spironolactone improved acne in women compared with placebo, offering an alternative to long antibiotic courses.

name: Rosacea
sx: Persistent redness of the cheeks, nose, chin and forehead
Easy flushing with heat, alcohol or spicy food
about: A chronic facial skin condition involving overactive blood vessels and inflammation, possibly aggravated by Demodex skin mites. In advanced cases the nose can thicken (rhinophyma). Unlike acne, there are no blackheads.

study.title: Treatment of rosacea by metronidazole
study.note: A small double-blind trial found metronidazole better than placebo for rosacea after 6 weeks, especially for papules and pustules.

name: Cellulitis
sx: A spreading area of red, warm, swollen skin
A break in the skin nearby
about: A bacterial infection, usually streptococci or staphylococci, of the deeper skin and fat beneath it, entering through cuts, cracks or athlete's foot. Doctors often draw around the red border to track whether it is spreading. Leg swelling makes repeat episodes more likely.

study.title: Compression Therapy to Prevent Recurrent Cellulitis of the Leg
study.note: In patients with chronic leg swelling and past cellulitis, compression therapy lowered recurrences compared with usual care in a small, single-center trial.

name: Impetigo
sx: Red sores that burst and form honey-colored crusts
Spreads easily to others, especially children
about: A highly contagious superficial skin infection, caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, common in young children. Bacteria enter through small breaks in the skin. Antibiotic creams usually clear it.

study.title: Fusidic acid cream in the treatment of impetigo in general practice: double blind randomised placebo controlled trial
study.note: Fusidic acid cream was much more effective than placebo for impetigo in general practice.

name: Scabies
sx: Intense itching that is worse at night
Thin wavy lines (burrows) on the skin
Rash between the fingers and on the wrists
Rash on the waist, armpits or genitals
about: Microscopic Sarcoptes scabiei mites burrow into the skin to lay eggs, and the itch is an allergic reaction to the mites and their waste, often starting weeks after infestation. It spreads by prolonged skin contact, so whole households are treated together.

study.title: Combined Oral Ivermectin and 5% Permethrin Cream to Treat Severe Scabies
study.note: A higher dose of ivermectin with permethrin cream was not better than the standard dose for curing severe scabies in adults.

name: Melanoma
sx: A mole with an irregular shape
A mole larger than about 6 mm or growing
A mole that changes, itches or bleeds
about: Cancer of melanocytes, the pigment cells of the skin, strongly linked to UV damage and sunburns. The ABCDE checklist (Asymmetry, Border, Color, Diameter, Evolving) helps spot it. Caught early it is usually curable by removal, but it can spread widely.

study.title: Individualised neoantigen therapy mRNA-4157 (V940) plus pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab monotherapy in resected melanoma (KEYNOTE-942): a randomised, phase 2b study
study.note: A personalized mRNA cancer vaccine (mRNA-4157) given with pembrolizumab prolonged recurrence-free survival after surgery for high-risk melanoma.

name: Vitiligo
sx: Often around the eyes, mouth, hands and joints
about: Immune T cells attack melanocytes, the pigment-making cells, through interferon-gamma and JAK signaling, leaving white patches. It is not contagious and doesn't hurt, but it can have a big psychological impact.

study.title: Two Phase 3, Randomized, Controlled Trials of Ruxolitinib Cream for Vitiligo
study.note: Ruxolitinib cream, a JAK inhibitor, restored more pigment than an inactive cream over 52 weeks.

name: Contact dermatitis
sx: An itchy red rash where the skin touched something
Blisters, sometimes in streaks or lines
Rash appearing hours to days after exposure
Dry, cracked skin with repeated exposure
about: Either direct irritation, as with soap or chemicals, or a delayed allergic reaction (type IV hypersensitivity) to a substance such as nickel, poison ivy oil (urushiol) or fragrances. The rash's shape often outlines the culprit, such as a watch strap. Patch testing identifies allergens.

study.title: Contact dermatitis to neomycin sulfate
study.note: Allergy to the antibiotic neomycin was rare in children having patch tests, and intermittent use on minor cuts was not linked to excessive sensitization.

name: Chickenpox (varicella)
sx: Itchy blisters appearing in crops, at different stages at once
Rash starting on the chest, back and face
about: Varicella-zoster virus spreads through the air and is highly contagious. Spots at different stages at the same time are a key clue. After recovery, the virus hides in nerve ganglia and can return decades later as shingles. Vaccination has made it far less common.

study.title: Immunisation of nurses with a live varicella vaccine
study.note: A live varicella vaccine was safe and produced immunity in seronegative nurses, while 6 of 7 unvaccinated susceptible nurses caught chickenpox from patients.

name: Mumps
sx: Painful swelling of the cheeks and jaw ('hamster face')
Painful swollen testicles in some males
about: A paramyxovirus that infects the parotid salivary glands in front of the ears. Complications include orchitis, meningitis and deafness. Outbreaks still occur in vaccinated groups with very close contact, such as university campuses.

study.title: Mumps outbreak in Orthodox Jewish communities in the United States
study.note: A large US outbreak spread through intense contact among schoolboys and overcame vaccine protection, but high two-dose coverage reduced severity and limited spread.

name: Hand, foot and mouth disease
sx: A rash or blisters on the palms and soles
A young child refusing to eat or drink
about: Caused by enteroviruses such as coxsackievirus A16 and enterovirus 71, it mainly affects children under 5 and spreads easily in childcare. It is usually mild, but enterovirus 71 can cause brain inflammation. It is unrelated to foot-and-mouth disease in livestock.

study.title: An inactivated enterovirus 71 vaccine in healthy children
study.note: An inactivated enterovirus 71 vaccine protected healthy children against EV71-related hand, foot and mouth disease.

name: Malaria
sx: Cycles of fever with shaking chills and drenching sweats
Recent travel to or living in a tropical region
Anemia and yellowing of the eyes
about: Plasmodium parasites, spread by Anopheles mosquito bites, multiply in the liver and then in red blood cells, bursting them in waves that cause the fever cycles. Plasmodium falciparum can kill within days. Artemisinin, discovered by Tu Youyou, who won a Nobel Prize in 2015, is the backbone of treatment.

study.title: Evidence of Artemisinin-Resistant Malaria in Africa
study.note: Confirmed that clinically artemisinin-resistant falciparum malaria had emerged independently and spread locally in Africa, a major threat to treatment.

name: Dengue fever
sx: Intense muscle and joint pain ('breakbone fever')
Bleeding gums or nose in severe cases
about: A virus spread by Aedes mosquitoes, with four serotypes. A second infection with a different serotype can be more severe, because existing antibodies can help the new virus enter cells (antibody-dependent enhancement). Severe dengue causes leaky blood vessels and shock.

study.title: Live, Attenuated, Tetravalent Butantan-Dengue Vaccine in Children and Adults
study.note: A single dose of the Butantan live dengue vaccine prevented symptomatic dengue (types 1 and 2) over 2 years, whether or not people had been infected before.

name: Cholera
sx: Massive, painless watery diarrhea like rice water
about: Vibrio cholerae bacteria release a toxin that makes intestinal cells pump out salt and water, so patients can lose liters of fluid a day. Oral rehydration solution, a simple mix of salt and sugar in water, is one of medicine's great life-savers. John Snow traced a London outbreak to the Broad Street water pump in 1854.

study.title: Cannabis, hypochlorhydria, and cholera
study.note: In volunteers given cholera or toxigenic E. coli, heavy cannabis use was linked to lower stomach acid and more voluminous diarrhea.

name: Tetanus (lockjaw)
sx: Painful muscle spasms triggered by noise or touch
A recent wound, especially a puncture
about: Clostridium tetani spores in soil enter through wounds and release tetanospasmin, a toxin that blocks the nerve signals that let muscles relax. Muscles lock in spasm. Vaccination and boosters prevent it, and neonatal tetanus is prevented by immunizing mothers.

study.title: Tetanus in Haiti
study.note: At a Haitian hospital, diazepam replaced older multi-drug regimens, good nursing and breathing support mattered most, and maternal vaccination cut neonatal tetanus admissions.

name: Rabies
sx: Fear of water: throat spasms when trying to drink
Tingling or pain at the site of an old animal bite
about: A lyssavirus in the saliva of infected animals, most often dogs worldwide and bats in the Americas, travels along nerves to the brain. Once symptoms start it is almost always fatal, but vaccine and antibodies given promptly after a bite prevent it. Louis Pasteur gave the first rabies vaccine to a bitten boy in 1885.

study.title: Post-exposure prophylaxis regimen of rabies monoclonal antibody and vaccine in category 3 potential exposure patients: a phase 4, open-label, randomised, active-controlled trial
study.note: Post-exposure prevention combining a rabies monoclonal antibody with vaccine was safe and protective, with long-lasting immune responses.

name: Acute HIV infection
about: In the weeks after infection, HIV multiplies rapidly and viral levels are very high, so people are especially infectious, while standard antibody tests may still be negative. Untreated, HIV destroys CD4 T cells over years, leading to AIDS. Modern treatment makes the virus undetectable and untransmittable.

study.title: Short-course antiretroviral therapy in primary HIV infection
study.note: A 48-week course of antiretroviral therapy started during primary HIV infection delayed disease progression, though not much beyond the treatment period itself.

name: Syphilis
sx: A painless, firm sore (chancre) where the infection entered
Weeks later, a rash on the palms and soles
about: Treponema pallidum, a spiral bacterium, passes through sexual contact. It is called 'the great imitator' because its later stages mimic many diseases, and untreated it can damage the brain, eyes and heart years later. A single penicillin injection cures early syphilis, and cases have been rising in many countries.

study.title: One Dose versus Three Doses of Benzathine Penicillin G in Early Syphilis
study.note: One dose of benzathine penicillin G was noninferior to three doses for treating early syphilis, judged by blood test response at 6 months.

name: Giardiasis
sx: After drinking untreated stream or lake water
about: The Giardia parasite clings to the lining of the small intestine and interferes with fat absorption. Its cysts survive in cold water, which is why hikers drinking from streams catch it. Lactose intolerance can linger after the infection clears.

study.title: Prepatency of giardiasis
study.note: In two-thirds of cases, symptoms had lasted over a week before the parasite could be found in stool, so repeated testing is worthwhile.

name: Rocky Mountain spotted fever
sx: High fever and severe headache after a tick bite
A spotted rash starting on the wrists and ankles and spreading inward
Rash on the palms and soles
about: Rickettsia rickettsii bacteria, spread by ticks, infect the cells lining small blood vessels and make them leak. Despite its name, it is most common in the southeastern and south-central United States. The antibiotic doxycycline should be started on suspicion, because delay can be fatal.

study.title: Rocky mountain spotted fever caused by blood transfusion
study.note: A case report documented Rocky Mountain spotted fever passed on through a blood transfusion from an infected donor.

name: Scarlet fever
sx: A red rash that feels like sandpaper
Flushed cheeks with pale skin around the mouth
Peeling skin on the hands and feet as it fades
about: Strep throat with a toxin-producing strain of group A Streptococcus whose toxin causes the rash. It was a major childhood killer in the 1800s and is now easily treated with antibiotics, but several countries saw resurgences in the 2010s.

study.title: Resurgence of scarlet fever in China: a 13-year population-based surveillance study
study.note: A 13-year national study found scarlet fever incidence in China rose substantially after 2011.

name: Toxic shock syndrome
sx: Low blood pressure, dizziness or fainting
Peeling skin on the palms and soles 1-2 weeks later
about: Toxins from Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus act as superantigens, switching on huge numbers of immune cells at once and causing a cytokine storm and shock. It became widely known in the early 1980s, linked to highly absorbent tampons.

study.title: Clinical manifestations of toxic shock syndrome
study.note: An early clinical description of toxic shock syndrome, noting that it then appeared to be mainly a disease of menstruating women, in whom it could recur.

name: Sepsis
sx: Fever or abnormally low temperature with shivering
Fast heart rate and fast breathing
about: Not an infection itself but the body's overwhelming response to one, which starts damaging its own organs. Every hour of delay in antibiotics raises the risk of death. Septic shock means blood pressure stays low despite fluids.

study.title: Effect of a Resuscitation Strategy Targeting Peripheral Perfusion Status vs Serum Lactate Levels on 28-Day Mortality Among Patients With Septic Shock: The ANDROMEDA-SHOCK Randomized Clinical Trial
study.note: In septic shock, guiding resuscitation by capillary refill time was not better than guiding it by lactate levels for 28-day survival (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK).

name: Conjunctivitis (pink eye)
sx: Discharge that crusts the eyelids shut overnight
about: Inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin membrane over the white of the eye, from viruses, bacteria or allergies. It is very contagious when infectious. Eye pain, light sensitivity or reduced vision suggest something more serious.

study.title: An outbreak of conjunctivitis due to atypical Streptococcus pneumoniae
study.note: A large conjunctivitis outbreak on a college campus was caused by an unusual unencapsulated strain of Streptococcus pneumoniae.

name: Acute otitis media (middle ear infection)
sx: A young child tugging at the ear
about: The middle ear fills with fluid behind the eardrum, often after a cold, and becomes infected. Children are prone because their eustachian tubes are short and nearly horizontal. Many cases clear on their own.

study.title: Tympanostomy Tubes or Medical Management for Recurrent Acute Otitis Media
study.note: For young children with recurrent ear infections, ear tubes did not lower the rate of infections over 2 years compared with medical management.

name: Botulism
sx: Drooping eyelids and blurred or double vision
Paralysis that moves downward from the head
In infants: constipation, weak cry and floppiness
about: Botulinum toxin, the most potent toxin known, blocks the release of acetylcholine at nerve endings, causing paralysis that descends from the head down. Sources include poorly home-canned food and, in infants, spores in honey, which is why babies under 1 shouldn't eat honey. Tiny doses are used medically as Botox.

study.title: Human botulism immune globulin for the treatment of infant botulism
study.note: Human botulism immune globulin was safe and effective for infant botulism, shortening hospital stays, costs and severity.

name: Typhoid fever
sx: A fever that climbs higher day by day
Abdominal pain and constipation or diarrhea
Faint rose-colored spots on the chest
A slow pulse despite high fever
about: Salmonella Typhi spreads through food and water contaminated with human feces. Some people become symptom-free carriers, most famously 'Typhoid Mary' Mallon, a New York cook in the early 1900s linked to dozens of cases. Drug resistance is growing.

study.title: Oral immunisation against typhoid fever in Indonesia with Ty21a vaccine
study.note: In Indonesia, the oral Ty21a vaccine partly protected against typhoid under intense transmission, but not against paratyphoid A.

name: Leprosy (Hansen's disease)
sx: Pale or reddish skin patches with loss of feeling
Numbness and weakness of hands and feet
about: Mycobacterium leprae grows best in cool parts of the body, the skin and peripheral nerves. Damaged nerves leave limbs numb, so unnoticed injuries cause deformity. Gerhard Hansen identified the bacterium in 1873. Multidrug therapy cures it, and most people are naturally immune.

study.title: Bedaquiline Monotherapy for Multibacillary Leprosy
study.note: Bedaquiline alone cleared Mycobacterium leprae within 4 weeks and improved skin lesions by 7 weeks in multibacillary leprosy.

name: Ebola virus disease
sx: Sudden fever, fatigue and muscle pain
Contact with a sick person or travel to an outbreak area
about: A filovirus spread through contact with the body fluids of infected people or animals. Fluid loss and damage to blood vessels cause shock. The 2014-2016 West African epidemic killed over 11,000 people. A vaccine and antibody treatments now exist.

study.title: A Randomized, Controlled Trial of Ebola Virus Disease Therapeutics
study.note: In the PALM trial, the antibody treatments mAb114 and REGN-EB3 lowered Ebola deaths compared with ZMapp.

name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
sx: Seeing halos or rainbows around lights
Red eye with a mid-sized pupil that doesn't react to light
about: The drainage angle at the front of the eye suddenly closes, so fluid can't escape and eye pressure soars, which can permanently damage the optic nerve within hours. It is more common in people who are farsighted, older and of East Asian descent. A laser hole in the iris prevents recurrences.

study.title: Laser peripheral iridotomy for the prevention of angle closure: a single-centre, randomised controlled trial
study.note: Among people with narrow drainage angles found by screening, laser iridotomy had a modest but significant protective effect, but disease was rare enough that widespread preventive treatment wasn't recommended.

name: Retinal detachment
sx: A sudden shower of new floaters
A shadow or curtain coming across part of the vision
about: The light-sensing retina peels away from the back wall of the eye, usually after a tear lets fluid seep underneath. Without its blood supply it stops working, so it is an emergency repaired by surgery. High short-sightedness and older age raise the risk.

study.title: Oral fluoroquinolones and the risk of retinal detachment
study.note: People taking oral fluoroquinolone antibiotics had a higher risk of retinal detachment, though the absolute risk was small.

name: Age-related macular degeneration
sx: A blurred or dark area in the center of vision
about: The macula, the part of the retina for sharp central vision, degenerates with age. In the 'wet' form, leaky new blood vessels grow beneath it and can be controlled with eye injections of anti-VEGF drugs. It is a leading cause of vision loss in older adults.

study.title: Intravitreal aflibercept 8 mg in neovascular age-related macular degeneration (PULSAR): 48-week results from a randomised, double-masked, non-inferiority, phase 3 trial
study.note: A higher dose of aflibercept kept wet macular degeneration under control with injections spaced further apart.

name: Cataract
sx: Glare and halos around lights, especially at night
about: Proteins in the eye's lens clump together and cloud it, mostly with age, though UV light, smoking, diabetes and steroids add to the risk. Cataract surgery replaces the lens with a plastic one and is among the most common operations worldwide.

study.title: Association Between Cataract Extraction and Development of Dementia
study.note: In a cohort study, cataract surgery was associated with a lower risk of developing dementia. The authors called for confirmation.

name: Hypothermia
sx: Shivering that stops as it worsens
about: Core body temperature falls below 35 °C (95 °F). As it drops, shivering fails, the brain and heart slow, and the heart can fall into a fatal rhythm. Some confused victims undress ('paradoxical undressing'). The rescue saying is 'nobody is dead until they are warm and dead'.

study.title: Resuscitation of an Unconscious Victim of Accidental Hypothermia in 1805
study.note: Described the successful rewarming of an apparently dead hypothermic man in 1805, showing that resuscitation is worth attempting even when it seems futile.

name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
sx: Several people or pets in the same house sick at once
Symptoms that improve when away from home
about: Colorless, odorless gas from faulty heaters, generators and engines binds to hemoglobin about 200 times more tightly than oxygen, starving tissues of oxygen. Pulse oximeters can falsely read normal. A home CO alarm is the best protection.

study.title: Hyperbaric oxygen for acute carbon monoxide poisoning
study.note: Three hyperbaric oxygen sessions within 24 hours reduced the risk of lasting memory and thinking problems after carbon monoxide poisoning.

name: Frostbite
sx: Numb, white or greyish-yellow skin on the fingers, toes, nose or ears
Skin that feels hard or waxy
about: Tissue freezes: ice crystals damage cells, and blood vessels clot, starving the area. Damaged tissue may take weeks to show its final extent, so amputation decisions are delayed. Refreezing after thawing is especially harmful.

study.title: Frostbite-A Case Series From Arctic Greenland
study.note: A case series from Arctic Greenland described frostbite injuries and their management, and discussed cultural reasons for a seemingly low incidence there.

name: Acute mountain sickness (altitude sickness)
sx: Headache after climbing above about 2,500 m
about: Thin air at altitude lowers blood oxygen. If the climb is too fast, the brain swells slightly and fluid shifts, causing symptoms. It can progress to life-threatening brain or lung swelling (HACE or HAPE). Ascending slowly prevents it, and descent is the cure.

study.title: Randomised, double blind, placebo controlled comparison of ginkgo biloba and acetazolamide for prevention of acute mountain sickness among Himalayan trekkers: the prevention of high altitude illness trial (PHAIT)
study.note: Among Himalayan trekkers, ginkgo did not prevent acute mountain sickness, while acetazolamide 250 mg twice daily gave strong protection.

name: Decompression sickness (the bends)
sx: Deep joint pain after a dive
Confusion or paralysis in severe cases
about: Nitrogen dissolves into tissues under pressure during a dive. If a diver surfaces too quickly, it forms bubbles, like opening a soda bottle, which block vessels and damage tissue. It was first described in bridge-building workers in pressurized caissons. Treatment is recompression in a hyperbaric chamber.

study.title: Patent foramen ovale and decompression sickness in divers
study.note: Divers with decompression sickness were far more likely to have a patent foramen ovale, a hole between the heart's upper chambers, suggesting it is a risk factor.

name: Lead poisoning
sx: Learning and behavior problems in children
A blue-grey line along the gums
about: Lead mimics calcium and disrupts enzymes, nerves and the making of hemoglobin. Children absorb more and their developing brains are most vulnerable. No safe blood lead level is known. Sources include old paint, contaminated water pipes and some imported products.

study.title: Association of dental caries and blood lead levels
study.note: Higher blood lead levels were associated with more tooth decay in the US population, possibly helping to explain regional and income differences.

name: Rickets
about: Children's growing bones can't mineralize properly without enough vitamin D, calcium or phosphate, so they bend under weight. Vitamin D is made in skin exposed to sunlight, so rickets was rampant in smoky industrial cities. Cod liver oil and fortified foods nearly eliminated it.

study.title: Florid and subclinical rickets among immigrant children in Glasgow
study.note: Found continuing florid and subclinical rickets among immigrant schoolchildren in Glasgow, and urged immediate action.

name: Beriberi (thiamine deficiency)
sx: Numbness and burning in the feet and legs ('dry' form)
Swelling of the legs and heart failure ('wet' form)
about: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is essential for turning carbohydrate into energy, so nerves and heart suffer first. It spread with polished white rice, which strips away the thiamine-rich husk. Christiaan Eijkman's chicken experiments on it earned a 1929 Nobel Prize. Today it is seen mostly with alcohol use disorder.

study.title: Thiamine deficiency and malaria in adults from southeast Asia
study.note: Thiamine deficiency commonly complicated acute falciparum malaria in Thai adults, especially severe cases, and could contribute to brain dysfunction.

name: Pellagra (niacin deficiency)
sx: A rash on sun-exposed skin, often around the neck (Casal's necklace)
about: Lack of niacin (vitamin B3) causes the 'four Ds': dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia and death. It swept the US South in the early 1900s among people living on untreated corn. Joseph Goldberger showed it was dietary, not infectious. Traditional nixtamalization of corn with lime releases its niacin.

study.title: Isoniazid-associated pellagra during mass scale-up of tuberculosis preventive therapy: a case-control study
study.note: In Malawi, mass use of isoniazid to prevent tuberculosis, combined with seasonal food scarcity, raised the risk of pellagra. Isoniazid interferes with niacin.

name: Vitamin A deficiency
sx: Foamy grey spots on the whites of the eyes (Bitot spots)
about: Vitamin A forms rhodopsin, the light-sensitive pigment in the rods used for dim-light vision, and maintains the eye's surface. Deficiency is a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide and raises deaths from measles and diarrhea. High-dose supplements are a cheap fix.

study.title: Maternal vitamin A supplementation and lung function in offspring
study.note: In an undernourished population, giving mothers vitamin A before, during and after pregnancy improved their children's lung function years later.

name: Kwashiorkor
sx: Swollen legs, feet and face despite malnutrition
about: A form of severe acute malnutrition in young children, classically after weaning, marked by swelling (edema) rather than visible wasting. The name comes from a Ga word from Ghana, often translated as 'the sickness of the deposed child'. Ready-to-use therapeutic food transformed treatment.

study.title: Intravenous Rehydration for Severe Acute Malnutrition with Gastroenteritis
study.note: In children with severe acute malnutrition and gastroenteritis, IV rehydration did not reduce deaths at 96 hours compared with oral rehydration.

name: Kawasaki disease
sx: Fever lasting 5 days or more in a young child
Red, cracked lips and a strawberry tongue
Swollen red hands and feet, later peeling
Rash and a swollen neck gland
about: An inflammation of medium-sized blood vessels in young children, first described by Tomisaku Kawasaki in Japan in 1967. Its cause is unknown. Untreated, it can cause aneurysms of the coronary arteries, and it is a leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries. IV immunoglobulin lowers that risk.

study.title: Efficacy of immunoglobulin plus prednisolone for prevention of coronary artery abnormalities in severe Kawasaki disease (RAISE study): a randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoints trial
study.note: In severe Kawasaki disease in Japan, adding prednisolone to immunoglobulin improved coronary artery outcomes (the RAISE study).

name: Sjögren's disease
sx: Dry mouth, trouble swallowing dry food
about: An autoimmune disease in which immune cells invade the glands that make tears and saliva. It mostly affects women and can occur alone or with lupus or rheumatoid arthritis. It raises the risk of lymphoma.

study.title: Safety and efficacy of subcutaneous ianalumab (VAY736) in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2b dose-finding trial
study.note: The antibody ianalumab produced a dose-related reduction in Sjögren's disease activity at 24 weeks, one of the first large trials in this disease to meet its main goal.

name: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)
sx: Thick, tight, shiny skin on the fingers and hands
Fingers turning white and blue in the cold
Small red spots on the face and hands
about: An autoimmune disease in which the body overproduces collagen, hardening the skin and sometimes the lungs, gut, heart and kidneys. Raynaud's phenomenon is almost always the first sign. Lung scarring is a leading cause of death.

study.title: Nintedanib for Systemic Sclerosis-Associated Interstitial Lung Disease
study.note: In lung disease linked to systemic sclerosis, nintedanib slowed the yearly decline in lung capacity compared with placebo, but did not help other features of the disease.
